Such susceptibility to superstition is difficult to reconcile with Sri Lanka’s claim to have preserved the Theravada Buddhist tradition for more than two millennia. If the country’s Buddhists, who constitute roughly two-thirds of the population, genuinely followed the Buddha’s core teachings, they would be less vulnerable to the perceived menace of Vas Kavi. In the Kalama Sutta, the Buddha famously advised the Kalamas not to accept a claim merely because it came from a religious leader, priest, teacher, elder, or member of the social elite. Rather, they were urged to examine it rationally and embrace it only if they judged that it would promote genuine social well-being

Vas Kavi culture

Sri Lanka has recently seen a surge in antagonistic poetry composed by anonymous individuals and crafted to appeal to a broad public audience. Known locally as Vas Kavi, these verses purport to summon malevolent forces against the country’s current rulers. They have spread rapidly across social media and are replayed by citizens constantly absorbed in smartphones, tablets, and computers. The phenomenon reflects the rise of the “screenager”—a term in contemporary British English for a generation engrossed in digital screens. Those who broadcast such provocative audio loudly in public, whether alone or in groups, have also attracted the disparaging British label “sodcasters.” In Sri Lanka, the trend suggests that people are using these viral verses both for emotional gratification and to give voice to fears buried deep within their minds.

The Vas Kaviya emerged alongside a Satyagraha campaign launched by a group of Buddhist monks demanding the release of a fellow monk sentenced to six years’ rigorous imprisonment for contempt of court. To rally public support for their cause, the participating monks walked the 115-kilometre Kandy–Colombo Road. When the march failed to produce the desired response, they gathered at Viharamahadevi Park, a public space intended for recreation and repose. There, they reportedly performed a ritual invoking Maha Sona, one of the fiercest demons in Sinhala folklore, to punish the rulers who refused to release the imprisoned monk unconditionally. A clay effigy of the ruler concerned was fashioned, and wooden nails were driven into it in Maha Sona’s name. Such acts are not Buddhist practices, but forms of primitive witchcraft passed down among the Sinhala people over millennia.

Roots of superstition in a Buddhist society

Such susceptibility to superstition is difficult to reconcile with Sri Lanka’s claim to have preserved the Theravada Buddhist tradition for more than two millennia. If the country’s Buddhists, who constitute roughly two-thirds of the population, genuinely followed the Buddha’s core teachings, they would be less vulnerable to the perceived menace of Vas Kavi. In the Kalama Sutta, the Buddha famously advised the Kalamas not to accept a claim merely because it came from a religious leader, priest, teacher, elder, or member of the social elite. Rather, they were urged to examine it rationally and embrace it only if they judged that it would promote genuine social well-being.

Yet many contemporary Buddhists in Sri Lanka do not follow this rational standard. Professor Kotagama Vachissara Thero, who taught Buddhist civilisation in 1960s at the former Vidyodaya University—the predecessor of today’s University of Sri Jayewardenepura—offered an explanation for this divergence. He observed that when Arhat Mahinda introduced Buddhism to ancient Lanka, the indigenous population worshipped trees and rocks. Rather than confronting and uprooting these deeply embedded practices, Arhat Mahinda introduced the Dhamma without violently disrupting the community’s existing beliefs.

The influence of these inherited beliefs remains visible today. Many Sri Lankans, when passing a large, spreading roadside tree, instinctively make an offering known as a panduru; others believe that a shrine built on a massive rock can confer divine favour. It is therefore unsurprising that Vas Kavi continues to inspire considerable fear among many Sri Lankans. I have seen older screenagers transfixed by their devices as they listen to these viral curses, uneasy smiles revealing a mixture of fear and fascination. Such reactions suggest how deeply this psychological vulnerability remains embedded in the nation’s cultural consciousness.

Mythological warfare in the digital age

The current Vas Kavi invokes a formidable demon king named Vajrapani to strike down a ruler accused of gaining power through falsehoods, although the intended target is deliberately left unnamed. Vajrapani is not a familiar figure in contemporary Sri Lankan folklore. The name combines vajra, the mythical diamond thunderbolt wielded by the deity Sakra, with pani, meaning the bearer or holder of that weapon. In Sri Lankan popular belief, whenever Buddhism faces an existential threat, Sakra is said to abandon his benevolent form and assume a terrifying demonic guise to destroy those who seek to undermine the faith.

In the viral composition, this fearsome manifestation of Sakra is invoked to destroy rulers whom the composer accuses of plotting against Buddhism. Educated observers may dismiss the verse as mythology or superstition. Yet its influence should not be underestimated in a society where such esoteric narratives continue to shape the collective imagination.

Epidemic of surface learning

Why do Sri Lankans so readily turn to such destructive invocations? One explanation is the modern retreat from the rational inquiry encouraged by the Kalama Sutta, which has weakened the public’s capacity for critical thought. Increasingly, people acquire information through shortcuts—glancing at social-media posts or listening to brief, catchy songs designed to capture attention and lodge in the mind. This is surface learning, the opposite of the deep learning society should cultivate. Because surface learning is effortless and undemanding, it encourages people to skim headlines and absorb impressions rather than investigate the underlying truth.

This intellectual complacency makes it easy for skilful manipulators to manufacture provocative headlines and circulate them widely. Nor is the drift towards surface learning confined to Sri Lanka; it has become a global concern. Educators in the Nordic countries and neighbouring Singapore have sought to counter it by renewing the emphasis on sustained reading and rigorous critical analysis—the foundations of deep learning. Sri Lanka is yet to announce the adoption of such a bold education reform. Instead, it worships AI and plans to introduce it as a facilitator of learning at schools. It is widely recognised that AI will stunt the development of human brain, though it can make it easy for teachers to assemble their teaching materials readily. 

In Sri Lanka, however, intense competition for admission to State universities encourages students to rely on surface learning at the expense of genuine understanding. Parents, anxious for their children to earn distinctions, often fail to create an environment that rewards curiosity and deep comprehension, despite their importance to long-term success. In reality, parents as a routine hire tuition masters to provide additional learning support to their children. Such tuition masters will help students to memorise answers to a given question selected by tuition masters from the past papers and do not help them to deep-learn a subject. These habits then follow students into adulthood and the workplace. 

Against this background, it is unsurprising that a myth-laden and superstitious Vas Kavi has gone viral: the public has been conditioned to embrace precisely such easily consumed material. When I asked several non-Buddhist friends whether they had listened to it, they said that although a notification had appeared on their smartphones, they had simply ignored it. Its circulation therefore appears to be concentrated mainly among Sri Lankan Buddhists—a troubling indication of the community’s future intellectual resilience.

Once the current International Monetary Fund (IMF) program ends, Sri Lanka’s leaders will face the formidable task of moving the country beyond its present fragile stability, placing it on a sustainable growth path, and strengthening its resilience to external economic shocks. Mobilising the public behind this national effort will be exceedingly difficult if one faction cultivates superstition while another responds with equally regressive tactics. Unless this cultural decline is reversed, it could seriously endanger the country’s economic and political future

Ideological enslavement and technical manipulation

The struggle, therefore, is fundamentally between surface learning and deep learning. Because surface learning demands little intellectual effort, the information it conveys is often fleeting and quickly forgotten. Those seeking to bind others to an ideology understand this weakness and exploit it by repeating the same message in varied forms until an idea first absorbed through a digital shortcut becomes embedded in the public consciousness. The technique recalls the methods of relentless repetition associated with Joseph Goebbels and wartime propaganda.

By repeatedly exposing the public to this Vas Kavi, its creators appear to be trying to lodge it in the nation’s collective consciousness. Yet, consistent with modern patterns of media consumption, even this feared verse has largely been absorbed at a superficial level. I asked several frequent listeners what it actually meant—whether they knew who Vajrapani was or why Sakra was believed to assume a demonic form to defend Buddhism from its supposed enemies. They could not answer. Their responses suggest that even superstition is now being consumed through the same effortless and uncritical habits that define the screen age.

I recently tested this phenomenon on an acquaintance’s birthday. I created a digital poster featuring her photograph and paired it with a song carrying a deliberately unconventional message: she needed no birthday wishes because her familiar smile showed that happiness was already a constant in her life. The poster also celebrated the dedication that had enabled her to rise professionally, captured in the Latin phrase Per Aspera Ad Astra— “through hardships to the stars”. The core message was that one should stand on his own feet for success without depending on gods, spirits, demons, and lowly-born spirits to deliver the same.

Within half an hour of being posted on Facebook, the image had attracted hundreds of “likes”. Yet this apparent engagement did not mean that viewers had understood its central message. The comments exposed the superficiality of their response: although the poster explicitly said that conventional birthday wishes were unnecessary, many viewers—including supposedly well-educated ones—posted routine “happy birthday” greetings or merely praised her smile. 

Few appeared to have read the message carefully. The episode offered a vivid demonstration of how screenagers consume content through surface learning. In a digital environment shaped by such uncritical habits, manipulators can readily fill the resulting intellectual vacuum and bind audiences to their preferred narratives.

Threat to national recovery

The immediate danger is that those targeted by the Vas Kavi may retaliate in kind, either by issuing a counter-curse or commissioning a Seth Kavi—a protective verse intended to shield them. Such rituals have no demonstrable physical effect: there is no evidence that a demon king named Vajrapani exists, that Sakra assumes a demonic form to defend the faith, or that supernatural forces can harm the unnamed ruler. The real danger lies instead in political factions answering superstition with superstition and drawing the country into an unproductive cycle of hostility. Such tribal confrontation could divert attention and energy from Sri Lanka’s fragile economic recovery.

No nation can progress while one part of its population is persistently pitted against another. Instead of strengthening the intellectual capacities needed for creativity, invention, and innovation, Sri Lankans risk becoming passive consumers of destructive, backward-looking content. For the country, this erosion of independent thought poses a profound threat to its future sovereignty and prosperity.

Once the current International Monetary Fund (IMF) program ends, Sri Lanka’s leaders will face the formidable task of moving the country beyond its present fragile stability, placing it on a sustainable growth path, and strengthening its resilience to external economic shocks. Mobilising the public behind this national effort will be exceedingly difficult if one faction cultivates superstition while another responds with equally regressive tactics. Unless this cultural decline is reversed, it could seriously endanger the country’s economic and political future.

Yet the country’s intelligentsia remains conspicuously silent. Academics and professionals must speak plainly: a nation at this fragile stage of recovery cannot afford further self-inflicted damage. They should unequivocally condemn both those who originated the Vas Kavi and those responding with retaliatory verses

A call to the intelligentsia and religious leaders

The emerging situation carries disturbing echoes of Sri Lanka’s catastrophic economic crisis in 2022, when the country exhausted its foreign exchange reserves and could no longer import even basic necessities. The resulting queues forced citizens to sacrifice millions of productive hours—a classic deadweight loss in which individuals, the economy, and society all suffered without any corresponding gain.

Yet the country’s intelligentsia remains conspicuously silent. Academics and professionals must speak plainly: a nation at this fragile stage of recovery cannot afford further self-inflicted damage. They should unequivocally condemn both those who originated the Vas Kavi and those responding with retaliatory verses.

Moreover, calling upon Sri Lanka’s Head of State to grant an unconditional pardon to a person convicted of contempt of court is inconsistent with established principles of good governance. Creating such a precedent would weaken confidence in the rule of law and deter legitimate investors from entering the country. If laws appear susceptible to pressure, reputable businesses will stay away, while those seeking to exploit institutional weakness will be encouraged to invest. The result would resemble Gresham’s Law, under which bad money—debased coins—drives good money out of circulation. In the same way, investors with questionable motives could displace the credible, long-term investment Sri Lanka needs.

The mainstream media likewise bears a heavy responsibility to foster deep learning rather than pursue sensationalist clicks. It must resist partisan alignment and confront the issue directly. Senior Buddhist leaders have an equally important duty—to safeguard both the integrity of the Dhamma and the welfare of the nation. If these influential institutions remain passive, the greatest burden will fall not on the elite but on Sri Lanka’s poorest and most vulnerable citizens, who will ultimately pay the price for this digital descent into superstition and tribalism.

(The writer, a former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, can be reached at waw1949@gmail.com )

title: Cleaner, but not yet cheaper to invest in: Sri Lanka’s anti-corruption gains and investment question | Daily FT

Sri Lanka has spent two years trying to convince the world that it is serious about corruption. There is progress to show on that front. There is less evidence that it has yet changed the country’s standing with foreign investors.

A reversal in the ratings

Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index scores countries from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (very clean). Sri Lanka’s score fluctuated between 36 and 38 from 2013 to 2019 and stood at 37 in 2021. Then it began to slide: 36 in 2022, 34 in 2023, with a rank of 115, and 32 in 2024. The 2024 rank of 121 was the worst on record. In 2025 the trend reversed. The score rose to 35, and the rank improved to 107.

Transparency International Sri Lanka cautioned against over-reading this. It said the 14-place jump overstates the improvement, since the underlying score rose by only three points. Perception indices also lag events, so the 2024 figure partly reflects the period before the change of Government.

Enforcement is visibly different

The sharpest change is in how the system treats powerful people. A retired High Court judge was appointed to head the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption in January 2025, and investigations and charges involving former ministers and senior officials followed. Parliament was told that 226 people were arrested between October 2024 and October 2026, including 55 politicians. The August 2025 arrest of former president Ranil Wickremasinghe was the first of a former head of state. Arrests are not convictions, and every case remains subject to due process.

Institutional reform is also moving. A beneficial ownership register was launched on 31 March 2026. The legal groundwork came earlier: the 2023 Anti-Corruption Act created the pathway the current Government is using. Assessments of that period were cautious about enforcement. The International Crisis Group argued that the Government’s reliance on the largest party in Parliament inhibited investigations into the powerful.

Questions remain on both sides. The Government’s opposition to a no-confidence motion against its energy minister damaged its reform credentials. Commentators have also warned that accountability for past wrongdoing must be matched by safeguards against abuse of state power.

What the investment figures show

Sri Lanka’s FDI figures are quoted on two different bases, which is why headlines differ. The international standard, used by the Central Bank, the World Bank, the IMF and UNCTAD, is net FDI on a balance-of-payments basis. It counts equity, reinvested earnings and inter-company debt, minus disinvestment. The Board of Investment instead reports gross inflows into its approved companies, including their foreign loans. This article uses the international measure.

On that measure, UNCTAD’s World Investment Report 2026 puts inflows at $1.044 billion in 2025, up from $759 million in 2024, an increase of about 38%. The Board of Investment’s own basis showed a 72% rise, because its 2024 base was lower. Inflows then settled at close to $200 million a quarter in the first half of 2026, on preliminary Central Bank figures.

That recovery is real but still below the pre-crisis peak. Net inflows reached about $1.6 billion in 2018, helped by one-off port deals, or about 1.7% of GDP. In 2025 they were about 1% of GDP. The inward FDI stock rose to $18.23 billion from $16.6 billion.

The rebound also looks modest beside the region. FDI into South Asia as a whole rose from $34.1 billion to $46.1 billion, a gain of about 35%, so Sri Lanka roughly kept pace with its neighbours rather than outpacing them. Bangladesh’s inflows rose 45% to $1.78 billion, while Pakistan received $1.85 billion, down from $2.67 billion in 2024. India’s inflows rose 44% to $39 billion. Sri Lanka accounts for only about 2% of the regional total. On World Bank data for 2024, Sri Lanka ranked 139th among 182 countries on net FDI as a share of GDP, against a global average of 4.25%.

What the data say about corruption and investment

A first-pass statistical analysis of Transparency International scores and Central Bank net FDI for 2016–2024 found only a weak link. The correlation was about 0.28 and statistically insignificant. Using the previous year’s score gave a result near zero. The score explained under 8% of the variation in FDI.

The explanation is visible in the series. The score moved by a few points over the decade, while FDI swung between about $430 million and $1.6 billion on its own schedule. The 2018 peak came from port-related deals. The 2019 fall followed the Easter attacks, and the 2020 low came with the pandemic. Inflows then recovered only partly after the 2022 sovereign default. The analysis cautions that nine annual observations make this indicative rather than a causal test.

What investors say holds them back

Investors’ stated concerns go beyond corruption. The US State Department’s 2025 Investment Climate Statement says FDI remains constrained, with most transactions in the $3 million to $5 million range. Despite the Government’s $5 billion FDI target for 2025, experienced investors say policy stability, regulatory reform and improved transparency must come first. The same assessment cites project reversals, regulatory shifts and slow decision-making. Adani Green’s February 2025 withdrawal from a $400 million wind project over contract renegotiation is often cited as an example.

The analysis adds that approval authority is spread across several agencies, so the Board of Investment struggles to act as a true one-stop shop. The Ease of Doing Business rank improved from 113th in 2014 to 99th in 2019. That fell short of the Government’s target of 70th, and the World Bank has since discontinued the index.

How the peers do it

Sri Lanka’s score of 35 is below the Asia-Pacific average of 45, but above Pakistan (28) and Bangladesh (24). It is also above the Sub-Saharan African average of 32, though behind Ghana’s 43.

Yet Bangladesh, with the weaker score, drew more FDI in 2025. The analysis attributes this to design rather than governance scores. Bangladesh runs export zones with ring-fenced customs and tax administration, and Vietnam courts investors through sector-targeted promotion and single-window licensing. Sri Lanka’s pitch, by contrast, has been generic and has shifted with each Government.

What would make the difference

The analysis proposes four steps. Each is a proposal, not a Government commitment.

Give the Board of Investment binding approval authority, with statutory decision deadlines of perhaps 30 to 45 days and a public dashboard of pending approvals.

Concentrate incentives and promotion on three or four sectors where the country has a real advantage, such as apparel, IT services, logistics and tourism-linked manufacturing.

Publish enforcement results and procurement and land-allocation scorecards for large investment projects.

Protect signed investment agreements in statute, so that a change of Government cannot reopen them.

The verdict

Sri Lanka has made real but early gains: a stronger law, visible enforcement, and a rebound in its score. Whether they are substantial will depend on court outcomes. The investment dividend has not yet arrived. FDI has recovered about as fast as the region’s, from a low base and still below its 2018 peak. The evidence suggests that faster approvals, targeted promotion and stable policy would matter at least as much as the score itself.

(The author is a Chartered Engineer)

title: Reflections from IMF and World Bank Annuals in Bangkok | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 03:03
-     - 15

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva (right)

World Bank President Ajay Banga (second from right)

Some global south governments, civil society, and think tanks, including Sri Lanka’s Institute of Political Economy, called for a different order of priorities, as many countries carry high debt-servicing obligations, poor public services, and lack access to adequate energy or water. They called for sufficient and predictable public finance to invest in health, education, energy, and food sovereignty. They raised the need for policy space to promote green industrial policies and to build the foundation for decent jobs for all

The 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group that completed in Bangkok, Thailand from 12 to 18 October, brought together over 15,000 participants from 191 member countries including policymakers, central bankers, ministers of finance and development, private sector executives, civil society representatives, journalists, and academics to discuss the state of the global economy and issues of international concern, such as the growth outlook, financial stability, rising inequality and poverty reduction.  

The Thai hosts welcomed participants with remarkable hospitality and efficiency despite the conditions under which dissent was permitted. Hundreds of local demonstrators marched near the National Convention Centre, protesting land rights impacts, carbon pricing models, and policies perceived to u foreign capital over local livelihoods.  Some made a strong case for a more fundamental reckoning: “Why Thailand Should Be Suing, Not Hosting the IMF.” The question was not rhetorical. It pointed to the land displacements, the conditionalities, and the structural adjustment legacies that have shaped Thailand’s own experience with the Bretton Woods institutions, and to the uncomfortable irony of a nation hosting the very architects of policies it has spent decades contesting.

The local protests reflected the wishes of many participants who were keen to see meaningful reforms to the International Financial Institutions that would place the wellbeing of people and the environment over returns on wealth and capital.

The status quo

Whilst multiple global issues require urgent action, cooperation was lacking at the event and reflected the geopolitically fragmented world. As the US pushes back on climate financing, points fingers at the “distorted policies” of other countries, and fights a war of choice, it produces the energy crunch and negative consequences.   IMF and the World Bank could and should have discussed the impact of these actions in a more insightful and meaningful manner. 

There was little self-reflection by the multilateral institutions on the policies and strategies that have contributed to the debt and economic crises facing many nations.   The Debt Report 2026 (Broad Global South) published by Erlassjahr, a German think-tank, identified 44 countries in the Global South suffering from a “very high foreign debt burden,” with another 25 heavily burdened and 15 at latent risk.  

Artificial Intelligence (AI) was the answer to almost every question on growth posed to the Bretton Woods institutions, even as they sidestepped the structural failures such as debt, austerity, and the chronic underfunding of public goods, that define the actual constraints on growth in the Global South. More than a dozen official panel discussions addressed AI, including one titled “What would it take?  Making Private Capital and AI Work for Countries”.  Another panel featured Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, as keynote speaker.  This came in the same week that the Booker Prize–winning author Arundhati Roy published an essay titled “Apocalypse Now and Then”, on the dangers of AI driving inequality, in which she writes: “It feels a little like that moment before the tsunami in 2004. Remember how, in Thailand and Indonesia, the ocean drew back from the coastline? People ran out to marvel at the miles of pristine new beach that suddenly emerged, not realising that, far out at sea, a wall of water was building up and would come crashing over them. We’re in that moment now. A towering wall of stupidity is about to inundate us.”

Benefits for the few

Private capital took centre stage at the World Bank Group, which claimed $112 billion was mobilised during fiscal year 2026 while offering no evidence on the number or quality of jobs created. 

Warnings of record debt were met with more fiscal consolidation, tight monetary stances for price stability, supply-side and structural reforms, and inflation targeting through central bank policies from the IMF rather than replenishing its Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, Resilience and Sustainability Trust, and Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust to ramp up much-needed financing.  It is disappointing that the international financial institutions have not been able to effectively replenish these specialised trust funds and financing vehicles managed by the IMF to support low-income and vulnerable economies.

Help for the many

Some global south governments, civil society, and think tanks, including Sri Lanka’s Institute of Political Economy, called for a different order of priorities, as many countries carry high debt-servicing obligations, poor public services, and lack access to adequate energy or water. They called for sufficient and predictable public finance to invest in health, education, energy, and food sovereignty. They raised the need for policy space to promote green industrial policies and to build the foundation for decent jobs for all.

The most important conversations happened outside the official meetings. From the Borrowers’ Platform to coordinate on debt and financial architecture, the Xingu Talks for aligning global finance flows, the Southern Caucus on sovereign industrialisation, the Feminist Festival of Resistance and Alternatives making a compelling case for a gender-just economy, and the International Peoples Assembly mobilising for economic, social, and climate justice, Global South governments and movements were building their own alternatives.

Their focus was policy sovereignty and a people-centred economy that values care and develops within planetary boundaries. These conversations reminded participants that alternatives are not only possible; they are already being imagined and built. There were calls for more grants and less debt, simple access, and faster disbursement.

The serious issues facing Sri Lanka’s economy and its people as a result of the unjust global economic order echo what is being raised across the Global South. There is an urgent need for the Government and civil society organisations to show solidarity by uniting and joining forces with other nations and activists to drive reforms within the international financial institutions, through active participation in the UNCTAD Borrowers’ Platform and the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, and by supporting the International Panel on Inequality, among other initiatives

Where are the alternatives?

Global debt and development campaigners such as Debt Justice UK, EuroDad, LatinDadd, Asia Peoples Movement for Debt and Development, AfroDad, Bretton Woods Project, MenaFem, IDEAs, Suramericana Vision, YukthiLk and numerous others, posed questions for finance policymakers. 

How can governments deal with the costs of today whilst protecting their ability to invest in tomorrow, at a time of limited fiscal space, high debt costs, energy and commodity price shocks, and the need to continue investing in health, education, climate resilience, and energy transition? How can debt governance incorporate external fiscal risks that affect debt sustainability but exist outside public borrowing? How can a new global standard on tax expenditure reporting, a vital step towards freeing up fiscal space, be introduced? And how can countries finance adaptation without worsening debt distress, external vulnerabilities, and pressures on essential public services?

Local alternatives

The serious issues facing Sri Lanka’s economy and its people as a result of the unjust global economic order echo what is being raised across the Global South. There is an urgent need for the Government and civil society organisations to show solidarity by uniting and joining forces with other nations and activists to drive reforms within the international financial institutions, through active participation in the UNCTAD Borrowers’ Platform and the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, and by supporting the International Panel on Inequality, among other initiatives.

The institutions that govern the global economy are structurally rigged against the South. Unilateral resistance is punished; collective action is shielded.  Unity also means building alternatives, not merely demanding seats at a table that was never designed for them but sharing the vast resources of technical expertise, policy solutions and collective experience available to drive essential changes to a world that rewards capital controlled by a few, over the work of the many.

(The author is a co-founder of the Institute of Political Economy (ipe-sl.org) and a former local councillor in London. He can be reached at charith@ipe-sl.org.)

title: Agentic AI: People and organisations at the crossroads | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 02:57

Ten years ago, I worked as the Chief Commercial Officer of a mid-size software company developing solutions for the BFSI sector. The word fintech was not so popular back then. RPA or Robotic Process Automation software was introduced in Sri Lanka during this time, and we opted to be a distributor for one of the three pioneering brands entered the market namely Blue Prism, UI Path and Automation Anywhere. RPA was ideal to automate processes of banks, insurance firms, and state authorities such as passport and border control handling large volumes of repetitive and rule-based tasks.  Fast forward, we now have AI enabled RPA which is an evolutionary leap beyond RPA and popularly known as Agentic AI that is going to make a big revolution in every industry across the world. This article aims to explain benefits, challenges and strategic directions for managers and business firms who will adopt Agentic AI in automating their workflows.

The profound use of AI 

AI has now become an everyday tool for most of the digitally literate individuals and tech savvy firms. Students, researchers, and employees of business firms use AI in their work with varying degrees of consent, competence and confusion. Many business firms allow employees to use AI as it can substantially improve productivity. Hours of coding work done by software engineers now happen in minutes. Teachers caution poor analytical skills and creativity among children due to heavy reliance on AI. Discussions between service providers and customers such as doctors and patients are becoming short and precise. Similarly, people are afraid of losing jobs as AI has become explosive filled with promises and fears.

Convergence of automation and AI 

RPAs were good in doing tasks but lacked thinking capability. AI particularly the LLMs or Large Language Models provide the ability to understand, logical reasoning, and plan. In other words, AI provides the brain. RPAs provide the ability to execute functions such as clicking a button, copying and pasting etc. The convergence of RPA and AI has given us real digital workers known as AI agents who can work like human employees. Agentic AI which comprises of multiple agents, can interact with different applications, manipulate data, manage and control hardware and execute tasks to achieve specific goals. Some argue that humans will work for machines in future. Humans losing control on fully autonomous systems can bring unprecedented threats to the world. Think of an era where power generation, irrigation management, air traffic control, border control etc. happen with no human intervention. Given these capabilities of Agentic AI, you may now think of the fate of BPO and KPO operations, service-oriented organisations and the back-office functions of top brands outsourced from developing countries.

Five levels of automation

The popular 2025 book by Pascal Bornet and his team on Agentic AI highlights its progress with five levels of automation. Level 1 describes rule-based automation, and this is what we had as RPA. Level 2 refers to intelligent automation. Levels 3 to 5 describe agentic workflows, semi-autonomous and fully autonomous agentic systems respectively. They emphasise the importance of starting automation at a low level in your organisation as it will enable you to be familiar with it, have control and governance mechanisms in place. This also shows the low control managers will have at higher levels of agentic automation and less instructions humans need to give.  The Cybercab by Tesla that has no steering wheel, pedals and mirrors is probably the latest and popular example for an autonomous agentic system.

Innovations in the era of Agentic AI

Unlike inventions, innovations need not to be grand discoveries and brand new to the world. If there is any sensible change, we make to a product or a process that can add value to stakeholders we can explain it as an innovation. It is stunning to see what Agentic AI can do in the wide array of innovation types and processes popularly in use such as incremental, radical, architectural, modular, disruptive, reverse, frugal, outcome driven and open innovation. As Agentic AI learns and improves what it does in each task, what we can expect is a dramatic push in all types of innovations. It is true that creativity is central to invent and innovate and we often tend to question the ability of machines to think creatively. Despite the algorithms and lines of codes or instructions they follow, machines are now capable of thinking. This flexibility in controls may lead to continuous incremental innovations in products and processes. We as human beings can have some protection until AI powered machines explore the exciting and uncertain world of disruptive innovations.  Some already highlight the enormous threats the world may face with super intelligence.

Dynamic capability embedded to DNA 

David Teece coined the term dynamic capability to remind organisations of the need to upgrade and update their capabilities in response to changes in the business environment. His latest articles and videos published in 2025 reemphasise the need of reconfiguring the capabilities of an organisation to remain competitive. Managers of all levels of a business firm, especially at the middle level, have this challenge of managing dynamic capabilities to ensure the organisation has an edge over competition and to accelerate innovations. Agentic AI being a practice that necessarily relies on learning from mistakes and constant learning for improvements, the future firms that are empowered with Agentic AI will have dynamic capabilities embedded to its DNA. This is no different to how culture is infused into the blood of an organisation.

Organisational inertia to fade away

People and organisations generally resist change. The preference to maintain the current equilibrium in the organisation known as the status-quo and rigid processes and procedures lead to organisational inertia that prevents change or makes it challenging. System integration is identified as the most challenging area business firms face when introducing AI Agents. Significant resistance may come from the technical people as the remedial measure involves ‘API first’ architecture. However, with more AI agents in use by business firms, managers may expect low inertia in future. One can argue that the level 3 Agentic workflows which is right now the most seen level of agentic automation will certainly result in low resistance to change.

Sustainability 

AI and Agentic AI require large amounts of resources. As highlighted in the AI Index Report 2026 by Stanford University, this is an industry which is scaling faster than surrounding systems around can adopt. Research and practices that aim to optimise resource utilisation include and are not limited to edge computing, fog computing, AI accelerators etc. Bio-inspired swarm intelligence and socially inspired intelligence are also popular areas for research. Increasing energy and water footprints, especially at data centers have become a major concern for governments and other interest groups. Given the speed of growth of AI, it is becoming important to monitor and regulate its purpose of use, the scope and cost before it is too late and irreversible.

Need for policy imperatives 

We often see in local media multiple initiatives by state authorities and think tanks on the way forward to a digital economy. Given that as a key goal in the national agenda, artificial intelligence particularly Agentic AI should necessarily be a focus area by policy makers and managers. Attempting to be competitive in regional or global markets without leveraging on agentic AI as a value driver will certainly be a costly lesson for everyone. 

Once again, we prove that we are quite slow in technology adoption as a nation in this massive transformation as well. We are behind many other nations, as highlighted in the AI diffusion report 2025 by Microsoft AI Economy Institute. State authorities, universities and business firms have a major role to play in increasing AI adoption for productive purposes.

Ethical perspectives in Agentic AI 

Top managers will face extremely challenging situations in adopting Agentic AI. The popular utilitarian way of deciding by looking at the consequences of a decision where pleasure for majority and pain for minority is the accepted norm cannot be easily applied here. One might argue that Agentic AI can enhance productivity and the broader society will benefit. Yet, at what cost is the question one needs to answer by looking at multiple stakeholders. A regular question I asked in my MBA classes for many years is who will need driverless cars and at what cost. Agentic AI systems are no different. Cost here is not only the cost of ownership and operations but also the social cost, impact on the environment, use of depleting resources and hidden losses in upstream and downstream activities. Surely, the excitement of a new technology cannot be at the cost of losing your job, water to drink and electricity for daily use. Hypercompetition may prompt business firms to resort to Agentic AI to get ahead. Managers need to think carefully about the quality of the decisions they make and the consequences, especially in the long run.

He is an ex-banker with several decades of experience in diverse industry sectors. He has been teaching organisational behavior, strategy and innovation management for over 25 years in postgraduate programs of 25 local and international universities. He could be reached via email shanta.y@sliit.lk)

title: Economic transformation in Asian countries and lessons for  Sri Lanka on new ways of earning | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 02:49
-     - 17

Whenever dollars run short, we borrow. We restrict imports. We restructure debt. We seek international help. These steps have saved us many times. Managing a shortage and ending it for good are two different jobs. We have done the first. We have hardly begun the second. So how does a nation end it for good? Some of our Asian neighbours found the answer. Their stories should give every Sri Lankan hope. Each of them lacked something the experts thought it needed. One was refused by the World Bank, others by the world’s biggest companies or by their own neighbours. None of them grew rich by doing more of what they already did. Each one found a new way to earn that nobody expected of it, and backed it with courage when others would not. Each one created an income that did not exist before. That is how their economic transformation started

Most of us still remember the queues of 2022 for fuel, gas, medicine and food, and the long nights of waiting, never knowing whether anything would be left by the time we reached the front. Shelves were empty because the country had run out of dollars. We promised ourselves then that it would never happen again. Yet history gives us reason to worry

Since 1965, Sri Lanka has entered into 17 lending arrangements with the IMF. Many brought reform, relief and recovery. Yet time and again, sooner or later, the shortage of foreign exchange returned. Before 2023, the last year Sri Lanka earned more from the world than it paid out to the world was 1977.

That is nearly half a century of living beyond our dollar income. A country cannot keep its promise to its children with borrowed dollars.

We have been managing shortages

Whenever dollars run short, we borrow. We restrict imports. We restructure debt. We seek international help. These steps have saved us many times. Managing a shortage and ending it for good are two different jobs. We have done the first. We have hardly begun the second.

So how does a nation end it for good? Some of our Asian neighbours found the answer. Their stories should give every Sri Lankan hope.

Written off by the world, they rose anyway

When Singapore left the Federation of Malaysia in 1965, few expected it to survive. It was a small island with no natural resources, no industry and limited land. It depended on the outside world even for its water, and unemployment was close to 9%. Three years later, Britain announced it would close its military bases on the island, which provided thousands of jobs. As much as a fifth of Singapore’s economy was put at risk. 

Singapore did not wait to be rescued. With no oil of its own, it built one of the three largest oil refining centres in the world. Its own Prime Minister later said the country had no natural advantage except that it had the idea and made it happen.

South Korea wanted a steel mill but had little iron ore of its own. The World Bank turned down its loan request and judged the plan premature. A consortium of seven Western steelmakers, formed to raise the capital, failed and was dissolved. Korea refused to give up. It turned to Japan, which agreed to lend most of the money. The Pohang mill poured its first iron in 1973, and within little more than a decade it was the biggest single steel plant in the world.

Korea’s leap into large shipbuilding followed the same path. Shipowners gave Korean builders a cold reception, and Japan refused to share its technology. Hyundai’s founder, Chung Ju-yung, travelled the world with a photograph of an empty beach in Ulsan and a 500 won banknote showing a turtle ship, a symbol of Korea’s shipbuilding past. A Greek shipowner took the risk and ordered two giant tankers. Hyundai broke ground in 1972. By 1983, it was the largest shipbuilder in the world.

In the late 1960s, Penang had lost its free port status and was suffering severe unemployment, with no natural resources to fall back on. In 1972, Malaysia opened its first free trade zone there, and Intel came the same year. Within three years, that one plant was doing more than half of Intel’s assembly work. Penang grew into one of Asia’s great electronics centres.

In the mid 1980s, Morris Chang set out to build a company that would make only chips designed by others, a business model the world had never seen. He asked Intel, Toshiba, Hitachi and Sony to invest. All of them said no. Only Philips came in from abroad, with Taiwan’s government as the largest shareholder. That company, TSMC, is now one of the most important manufacturers on earth.

Around the same time, Gulf Air cut back its services to Dubai. Dubai answered by starting an airline of its own. Emirates flew its first flight in 1985 with a handful of aircraft and $10 million in start-up funding. The same year, Dubai opened the Jebel Ali Free Zone with just 19 companies. Today the zone hosts more than 11,000 businesses, Emirates is one of the world’s largest international airlines, and oil, once a third of Dubai’s economy, has shrunk to a tiny share of it.

What they had in common

Look closely, and a pattern appears. Each of them lacked something the experts thought it needed. One was refused by the World Bank, others by the world’s biggest companies or by their own neighbours. None of them grew rich by doing more of what they already did.

Each one found a new way to earn that nobody expected of it, and backed it with courage when others would not. Each one created an income that did not exist before. That is how their economic transformation started.

Why not Sri Lanka?

Now think of what we start with. Sri Lanka has more land, more natural resources and more people than Singapore had in 1965. We sit beside one of the busiest east-west shipping routes in the world. Our people are educated and skilled, and hundreds of thousands of Sri Lankans work and build businesses across the globe. Our exporters have shown for decades that they can compete with the best.

If Singapore could build a refining industry without a drop of oil, and Korea a steel industry with little iron ore, what could Sri Lanka build with everything it already has?

The answer may already exist. It may be in the mind of an engineer in Colombo, a university student in Kandy, a teacher in Jaffna, an entrepreneur in Galle or a Sri Lankan professional in London. The next billion dollars may be sitting in an idea that no decision maker has heard yet.

Sri Lanka has every reason to follow the Asian path, and no reason to be the exception.

The clock is already running

Hope alone will not do it. Neither will plans that stay on paper. New earnings take years to mature. Hyundai needed eleven years to go from an empty beach to the top of world shipbuilding. The dollars Sri Lanka will need in the 2030s must be planted now and nurtured.

The signs of need are already here. 2025 gave us real reasons to feel proud: record remittances above $8 billion, tourism earnings of about $3.2 billion and a third year of current account surplus. The Government’s discipline deserves credit for this, and many began to feel the danger had passed.

2026 has reminded us how quickly the picture can change. With the conflict in the Middle East pushing up costs, the current account slipped back into a deficit of $291 million for January to August. The merchandise trade deficit widened to $7.2 billion, from $4.3 billion a year earlier. Tourist arrivals fell. By the end of September, the rupee had lost 6.3% against the dollar since the start of the year.

There are quieter signals too. The dollars the Central Bank bought from the market fell from $1.76 billion in the first half of 2024 to $0.56 billion in the first half of 2026. And the IMF’s latest review assumes Sri Lanka will return to international bond markets for $3 billion in 2027 and 2028. The Government has rightly said these are the IMF’s assumptions, not its own projections. But the assumption tells us something important: unless new earnings grow fast enough, borrowing remains the default way to fill the gap.

Our reserves of around $6.9 billion have been rebuilt with great care. But reserves are savings, not income, and our traditional earners each depend on things we do not control, from jobs in other countries to peace in the wider world. Hoping they will be enough is not a plan.

Every new dollar we earn is a dollar we will not need to borrow.

The door is already open

On 22 September, the National Business Facilitation Centre, ViYASA, opened under the Presidential Secretariat, built on the President’s own concept. Its purpose is to clear the administrative and regulatory barriers that slow down investment and business. This is a far-sighted step, and it deserves the support of every Sri Lankan who wants this country to succeed.

Here lies a rare opportunity. Most new earning ideas need several institutions to say yes. They belong to no single ministry, so for decades they have had nowhere to go. Many simply died on a desk. The Centre sits above those divisions. It can become the national home for new foreign exchange earning and saving pathways, alongside its work of removing bottlenecks.

By now, the Centre may already have received proposals for new ways of earning foreign exchange. Some of those may be substantial foreign exchange inflow pathways holding the first seeds of Sri Lanka’s own transformation.

Giving the Centre the role of evaluating these ideas and helping them through to activation could be set in motion in the fewest working days possible. The door the President has opened can become the door through which Sri Lanka walks out of its dollar trap for good.

A call to the Chambers of Commerce and Industry and to every Sri Lankan

Some of our most valuable ideas can come from people who have never sat in a planning meeting.

To our chambers of commerce, trade associations and professional bodies: call your members together, hold brainstorming sessions, sift the ideas and bring the strongest ones to the Centre. One good idea, carried forward by a chamber with the weight of its members behind it, can open new dollar income paths that no single company could open alone.

To our universities: which services could your faculties sell to the world? To Sri Lankans working overseas: which partners and markets could you bring home? To our industrialists: what could we make here that the world would buy, or that we now import without need?

You do not need a detailed feasibility study to start. You need an idea, and the courage to put it forward. Start today: write your idea down, talk it over with your chamber or professional body, and have it ready to submit. Every Sri Lankan who brings a workable idea becomes part of building the country’s future.

Facilitating business and removing bottlenecks is exactly the help most new foreign exchange earning paths will need, so in spirit they already belong within its work. But what is implied is easily overlooked; what is assigned gets done. What remains, then, is a small decision with a very large reach: to name the receiving and activating of new foreign exchange earnings and saving paths as a specific mandate of the Centre, assign it as a direct responsibility, and allow the whole nation to take part. This does not replace any existing policy. It adds to what is already being done. It does not cost the Treasury a fortune. It costs only attention, and the will to act before the next storm rather than during it. Each of the Asian transformations described here began with a bold decision, taken early and carried through with courage

To the President and those who decide

The hardest step, creating the Centre, has already been taken. Facilitating business and removing bottlenecks is exactly the help most new foreign exchange earning paths will need, so in spirit they already belong within its work. But what is implied is easily overlooked; what is assigned gets done.

What remains, then, is a small decision with a very large reach: to name the receiving and activating of new foreign exchange earning and saving paths as a specific mandate of the Centre, assign it as a direct responsibility, and allow the whole nation to take part.

This does not replace any existing policy. It adds to what is already being done. It does not cost the Treasury a fortune. It costs only attention, and the will to act before the next storm rather than during it. Each of the Asian transformations described here began with a bold decision, taken early and carried through with courage.

Because new earnings take years to mature, every month we wait today becomes a month of shortage in the years ahead. The best answer to any bond assumption is a pipeline of new earnings strong enough to make it unnecessary.

Imagine a Sri Lanka where anyone with an idea that could earn the country a dollar knows exactly where to take it. Imagine our children growing up never knowing what a fuel queue or fuel quota looks like.

That is a legacy worth building. One day, other nations may tell Sri Lanka’s story the way we now tell Singapore’s and Korea’s. And it must begin now. Let us keep doing well what we already do. But let us also give the whole nation a reason, and a place, to discover what we have not yet begun to do.

After decades of spending more than it earned, it is time Sri Lanka opened innovative new pathways for more dollars to flow in than the country needs for spending.

(The author, CEng FIMechE FIET (UK) CEng FIE (SL), is Founder and Chairman of the KIK Group of Companies, an export-oriented engineering and switchgear assembly manufacturer and a Presidential Export Award winner, and serves on the Executive Committee of the Free Trade Zone Manufacturers’ Association of Sri Lanka. The views expressed are his own. He can be reached at lalith@kik.lk.)

title: Port Unions appeal to President to allow ECT to be operated by SLPA | Daily FT

In these circumstances, a decision to transfer the operation of the East Container Terminal to a private party would deprive the people of Sri Lanka of the full benefits of an investment made with public funds. Giving ECT to a second operator would mean making a substantial investment to develop a major strategic national asset without enabling the Sri Lanka Ports Authority to obtain the full benefits of its operations and commercial potential

The Joint Executives’ Alliance of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority (EAPA), comprising the Staff Officers’ Association of the SLPA and Engineers’ Association of the SLPA, have written to President Anura Kumara Dissanayake to retain the Colombo East Container Terminal under the full ownership and direct operational control of the SLPA. Following is the text of the letter signed by SLPA Staff Officers’ Association President C.D. Jayasekara, SLPA Engineers’ Association President K.C.M. Wanasinghe, Secretary M.M.S.R. Silva. and SLPA Staff Officers’ Association Secretary W.K.P. Suranga Walpola

We respectfully submit this letter to express our serious concern regarding the recently announced proposal to hand over the operations of the East Container Terminal (ECT) to a private party. By the way doing so, we draw your attention to the terminal’s operational readiness, financial strength, and long-term strategic significance, matters about which we have previously expressed concern. We firmly believe that the East Container Terminal, as a strategic asset belonging to Sri Lanka, should remain under the full ownership and direct operational control of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA).

ECT is not merely another container terminal. Situated within the Port of Colombo, it is a nationally significant strategic asset capable of safeguarding the future competitiveness of our port and further strengthening the contribution made by the Sri Lanka Ports Authority to the national economy.

Sri Lanka has invested in ECT; securing its full benefits is the responsibility of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority

The Sri Lanka Ports Authority has already made substantial investments in developing ECT, using its own financial resources. Through this public investment, the terminal’s infrastructure, modern equipment, and automation systems have been developed, with the objective of establishing a modern, semi-automated container terminal capable of competing with the world’s leading terminals.

The principal capital investments in this project have now been completed. Major facilities already in place include 12 ship-to-shore gantry cranes, 40 automated rail-mounted yard gantry cranes, the Navis N4 terminal operating system, the ABB automation platform, and the operations building.

Over the past several years, the operations and engineering teams of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority have worked with continuous dedication to prepare operational and human-resource plans, study workflows, integrate systems, and overcome technical challenges. Through these efforts, employees and management of the Authority have made a substantial contribution towards bringing this terminal into operation.

The terminal’s major investments have already been made, and the remaining commissioning and system-activation work is expected to be completed by the latter part of 2026. In these circumstances, a decision to transfer the operation of the East Container Terminal to a private party would deprive the people of Sri Lanka of the full benefits of an investment made with public funds.

The strongest argument for a new container terminal being operated successfully under public management is provided by the operational history of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority itself. By successfully operating the Jaya Container Terminal (JCT), the Authority has demonstrated its ability to compete with private-sector terminals and to manage operations efficiently and profitably. In 2014, the JCT operated by the Sri Lanka Ports Authority handled 2.56 million TEUs of containers. Similarly, since 2010, JCT, a terminal under SLPA management, has handled an average annual container volume exceeding 2 million TEUs

Sri Lanka Ports Authority has a proven ability to operate ECT successfully

The strongest argument for a new container terminal being operated successfully under public management is provided by the operational history of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority itself. By successfully operating the Jaya Container Terminal (JCT), the Authority has demonstrated its ability to compete with private-sector terminals and to manage operations efficiently and profitably.

In 2014, the JCT operated by the Sri Lanka Ports Authority handled 2.56 million TEUs of containers. Similarly, since 2010, JCT, a terminal under SLPA management, has handled an average annual container volume exceeding 2 million TEUs.

The Sri Lanka Ports Authority’s operating division has already developed the operational experience, human resources, financial resources, and system-integration capabilities necessary to make ECT operational. These achievements also demonstrate the terminal-operations experience required for future challenges.

The financial benefits are clearly demonstrated

As the Sri Lanka Ports Authority is a Government institution that pays dividends to the Treasury, its financial success is also directly connected to the public interest of Sri Lanka. It is a profit-making state institution that contributes to the national economy through the effective operation of its terminals.

According to the Sri Lanka Ports Authority’s own figures, during 2021–2025, the JCT terminal alone generated a total profit of Rs. 63.2 billion for the Sri Lanka Ports Authority. In comparison, the combined income generated by the two terminals, SAGT and CICT, for that period amounted to Rs. 62.5 billion.

Furthermore, between 2019 and 2025, the State-owned JCT terminal paid a total of Rs. 14.6 billion in dividends, while the contribution from the CICT terminal was Rs. 1.4 billion. Thus, JCT’s contribution was more than ten times that of CICT.

These figures make clear the real economic value of operating a terminal under SLPA control. The Authority estimates that operating ECT at full capacity could generate approximately $ 200 million in annual income for the port.

While all income earned by a state-owned terminal becomes part of Sri Lanka’s financial system, a considerable portion of the revenue received by a privately operated terminal flows overseas through financial arrangements. In contrast, income generated by a fully State-operated terminal remains within the country and directly supports the national economy.

By operating ECT directly, the Sri Lanka Ports Authority has the ability to strengthen its operating efficiency, future port development, infrastructure, modernisation, and training. Therefore, rather than simply transferring operations to a private party, the Authority should be given the opportunity to develop the terminal itself and obtain the benefits of its investment.

Consequently, when evaluating the proposed ownership and operating arrangement, it is not sufficient to consider only the income that the Sri Lanka Ports Authority may receive. It is also essential to consider the value that would be surrendered, the operational authority that would be lost, and the long-term financial returns.

The proposed model risks weakening the strategic future of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority

Your Excellency, we wish to draw your attention to an important matter concerning port ownership. Although the Sri Lanka Ports Authority would retain ownership of the port’s property, allowing a private operating party to take control of daily operations and the port’s strategic direction could undermine the Authority’s position.

Giving ECT to a second operator would mean making a substantial investment to develop a major strategic national asset without enabling the Sri Lanka Ports Authority to obtain the full benefits of its operations and commercial potential.

Regarding container-handling volumes, Your Excellency has stated that ECT currently handles approximately 0.5 million TEUs, and the view has been expressed that this volume could increase under private-sector management. However, the essential additional equipment has already been ordered but has not yet arrived. Therefore, regardless of who the operator is, ECT cannot at present function at its complete design capacity. Once the equipment is received, the SLPA will be ready to operate ECT at its full capacity, with the potential to reach 3.5 million TEUs annually. In the meantime, SLPA operating teams have been carrying out operations in stages and conducting tests under the available conditions.

ECT’s modern infrastructure, deep-water facilities, and its potential for an additional 800-metre expansion under the North Port project make the terminal extremely important for the next stage of growth of the Port of Colombo. Accordingly, this decision is directly linked to the future of the SLPA’s container-terminal business.

Projected growth of ECT container-handling volumes under the Sri Lanka Ports Authority

If direct operational control of ECT is taken away from the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, it may lose the capacity to compete commercially in the future, maintain its long-term financial stability, and finance future national port development. It is a risk that should not be taken lightly.

Moreover, ECT, when operated by the Port Authority, can function neutrally and openly for all shipping lines. Without depending on a particular shipping line or alliance, it can provide all operators with fair commercial access. This would serve the wider national interest and further strengthen the status of the Port of Colombo as a regional maritime hub.

The tender for the remaining equipment is already under way

The purchase of the remaining equipment needed to commence operations at the East Container Terminal, including SC equipment, is currently required. Steps have already been taken to coordinate this process with ECT’s public-sector operating division, and tenders have been called for that purpose. It is understood that several domestic and foreign bidders have expressed interest.

In addition, attention has been drawn to delays in tender procedures for the purchase of Straddle Carriers. Although there have been such delays, the required equipment can be procured through an accelerated process, and ECT can be brought into successful operation without unnecessarily extending the timetable. The relevant equipment specifications and requirements have already been prepared.

The Sri Lanka Ports Authority already possesses the principal infrastructure and operational capabilities required for ECT. Through proper coordination of the procurement of the remaining equipment, the implementation of the system can be accelerated. Handing the terminal to an overseas or private operator merely because its immediate operational income is lower would be a decision that overlooks the substantial public investment already made. Therefore, priority should be given to enabling ECT to operate successfully under SLPA control, so that the full returns on investment can benefit the nation.

During 2021–2025, the JCT terminal alone generated a total profit of Rs. 63.2 billion for the Sri Lanka Ports Authority. In comparison, the combined income generated by the two terminals, SAGT and CICT, for that period amounted to Rs. 62.5 billion. Furthermore, between 2019 and 2025, the State-owned  JCT terminal paid a total of Rs. 14.6 billion in dividends, while the contribution from the CICT terminal was Rs. 1.4 billion. Thus, JCT’s contribution was more than ten times that of CICT. These figures make clear the real economic value of operating a terminal under SLPA control. The Authority estimates that operating ECT at full capacity could generate approximately $ 200 million in annual income for the port

Private-sector participation is not indispensable

The Sri Lanka Ports Authority is not opposed to private-sector participation in the development and operation of container terminals at the Port of Colombo. In fact, the WCT II project and the proposed North Port development could be implemented through suitable public-private partnerships (PPPs), where appropriate.

There are also occasions when partnerships with the private sector are needed to carry out major new investments that the government cannot finance on its own. However, the East Container Terminal (ECT) is a different situation. Approximately 99% of the overall project cost has already been financed by the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, and the funds required to complete the remaining investment by the end of 2026 have also been allocated. Therefore, at this stage, transferring the operation of this terminal to a private party cannot be justified solely on the basis that private-sector investment is essential.

The strategic decision that needs to be taken at this final stage

Your Excellency, the real need at present is not to identify a new operator for the terminal but to allow the Sri Lanka Ports Authority to complete the commissioning of ECT successfully.

Investments have already been made, the principal infrastructure and equipment have been established, human resources have been prepared, employees have been recruited, and operating teams have gained experience. We stand ready to make an active contribution to the successful completion of this task.

Therefore, we firmly believe that giving the organisation that financed, developed, and prepared this terminal the opportunity to complete this work and lead its operations would be the more appropriate strategic decision.

Accordingly, Your Excellency, we respectfully submit the following requests:

1. That the proposal to transfer the operations of ECT to a private party be withdrawn and that the continuation of ECT under the full ownership and direct operational control of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority be assured.

2. That the Sri Lanka Ports Authority be given the opportunity to obtain the full economic benefits of the investment already made, strengthen its financial stability, make a meaningful contribution to the Treasury, and develop ECT as a strategic national asset capable of contributing to the future port development of Sri Lanka. 

Your Excellency, the ECT is not merely a port facility. It is a massive investment made by the people of Sri Lanka, a commitment by the staff of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, and a strategic

opportunity acquired by Sri Lanka. At this decisive stage, we believe that allowing the Sri Lanka Ports Authority itself to carry the investment forward will help preserve a national asset that can serve future generations.

We respectfully request that this matter be given your close attention in view of the long-term benefit of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, the Port of Colombo, and the people of Sri Lanka. We also request an opportunity for a discussion with all the parties involved. We wish to respectfully inform you that the Joint Executives’ Alliance is prepared to provide further clarification and the necessary technical information regarding the implementation of the terminal.

title: A one-way strait: The equity anomaly sabotaging Indian investments into logistics | Daily FT
summary:

By An Indian cargo operator

Sri Lanka’s transhipment engine is fundamentally fuelled by Indian cargo, yet an asymmetrical regulatory wall restricts Indian logistics companies from fully participating in the island's domestic market. While Colombo Port thrives as a primary maritime gateway for the Indian subcontinent, a protectionist legacy in Sri Lanka's shipping and logistics sector creates a striking policy anomaly. Sri Lankan firms enjoy the freedom of 100% equity ownership in India's logistics sector, but India and all other foreign nations face a strict 40% foreign equity cap for freight forwarding and shipping agencies in Sri Lanka.

This imbalance presents a structural bottleneck for an island striving to evolve from a basic transhipment stop into a comprehensive regional logistics hub. Without Indian manufacturing and consumer demand, Sri Lanka’s multi-billion-dollar port infrastructure would operate at a fraction of their capacity. Sri Lanka secures immense port revenues and economic stability because of the Indian economic output yet controls the cargo with protection for few operators discouraging investments.

Discussing the subject openly itself is not encouraged and is stopped or targeted by the oligopoly lobby of the Sri Lankan shipping and logistics industry. The Government of Sri Lanka has continuingly been misled by a few personnel who have direct access to the president’s office under any government for decades and stops legal reforms and modernisation.

The transhipment dependency and support for export growth

Sri Lanka’s maritime success is inextricably linked to its northern neighbour. The country sits strategically along the crucial East-West shipping lane, positioning it perfectly to handle the overflow and consolidation of South Asian trade. The Indian share: Approximately 70% to 75% of Colombo Port's total transhipment volume consists of cargo originating from or destined for India. However, the location has served less over the years and due to lack of scalable choice Sri Lankan exporters and logistics companies are losing competitiveness rapidly under few oligopolistic agency houses controlling logistics technical making it more expensive for cargo movements as its strives competition

The ownership anomaly

Despite this heavy reliance on Indian trade to sustain its maritime and logistics ecosystem, Sri Lanka enforces a strict, protectionist regulatory framework. Under long-standing domestic laws, foreign ownership in shipping agencies and freight forwarding companies is restricted to a maximum of 40%, requiring a 60% local majority partner.

The paradox sharpens when looking across the Palk Strait. Under India's liberalized foreign direct investment (FDI) guidelines, Sri Lankan companies can hold 100% equity ownership in Indian shipping, logistics, warehousing, and freight operations under the automatic route. Sri Lankan logistics giants have actively utilized this open-door policy, successfully scaling up vast networks within mainland India.

For Indian operators, however, setting up an end-to-end network in Sri Lanka remains legally impossible without diluting their equity and surrendering corporate control to local partners who rely on Indian cargo to run their business.

The risk of holding back liberalisation

Maintaining this regulatory asymmetry poses a severe long-term risk to Sri Lanka’s maritime and logistics dominance. While local oligo lobbyists push for the 40% cap since the 1970’s closed economic model the world has moved on, and all global hubs now have an open-door policy in the sector attracting billions of dollars as FDI. The Sri Lankan protection simultaneously deters global players from making deep capital commitments in value-added logistics infrastructure into Sri Lanka keeping it locked in as a regional transhipment port and affects its export competitiveness directly.

Furthermore, Colombo policy makers must remember, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been very strategic since he took office in 2015 with a maritime and logistics strategy which is aggressively developing its own maritime and logistics infrastructure with fast reforms. The expansion of direct mainliner services to Indian ports, reforms in cabotage laws, and the construction of deep-water transhipment ports and new logistics centres within India. This means that dependence on Colombo is no longer a permanent necessity for Indian cargo and no Indian company will promote Sri Lanka as a logistics centre with a cap on freight forwarding and shipping.

If Sri Lanka wishes to anchor Indian cargo to its shores permanently, it must move beyond simply acting as a transhipment pitstop. Reciprocal liberalization allowing Indian and international players the corporate security of full ownership. This is the missing link required to transform Sri Lanka into a truly competitive, world-class Indian Ocean logistics hub. Not its location.

The Indian cargo operators in Colombo request the Indian Government’s attention and request its High Commissioner Santosh Jha to take up the serious anomaly in policy with the Government of Sri Lanka.
