By Hishan Welmilla

Sri Lanka concluded its campaign at the 5th Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, finishing 16th in the overall medal table with two gold, four silver and three bronze medals. The nine-medal haul highlighted the country’s continued competitiveness in para-athletics and swimming, with record-breaking performances from Pradeep Somasiri and Janani Dhananjana emerging as the major highlights of the Sri Lankan contingent.

Distance runner Pradeep Somasiri delivered one of the most outstanding performances of the Games, winning gold in the men’s T46 1,500 metres with a time of 4:03.25, establishing a new Games record. His victory demonstrated his endurance, tactical awareness and ability to maintain a strong pace before producing a decisive finish. Somasiri had also won gold in the same event at the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, China, where he clocked 4:05.14. Improving his previous Games record by 1.89 seconds in 2026 underlined his continued development and consistency at the highest level of Asian para-athletics.

Janani Dhananjana also experienced disappointment in the women’s T47 100 metres, finishing fourth in the final with a time of 12.60 seconds. She narrowly missed the podium in a competitive race won by China’s Jie Shan in 12.36 seconds. However, Dhananjana responded impressively to the setback, winning silver in the women’s 200 metres before securing gold with a Games-record leap of 5.52 metres in the long jump. Her ability to recover from the disappointment of missing out on a medal in the 100 metres and go on to win two medals demonstrated her versatility, resilience and competitive determination.

Nuwan Indika Gamage added a silver medal in the men’s T44 100 metres, recording a season-best time of 11.58 seconds. Although he had won gold in the same event at the 2023 Asian Para Games with a time of 11.63 seconds, his faster performance in 2026 was not enough to secure the title. His result nevertheless demonstrated his continued sprinting ability and competitiveness against Asia’s leading para-athletes.

Palitha Bandara also secured silver in the men’s F42 shot put with a throw of 14.02 metres. Having won bronze in the event at the 2023 Games, Bandara improved his medal standing in 2026, reflecting his strength, throwing technique and consistency in a highly technical discipline.

Sri Lanka’s remaining medals came from a combination of athletics and swimming. Galina Basnayake won silver in the women’s S9 400 metres freestyle, demonstrating her endurance and ability to sustain an effective pace over a longer distance. Naveed Raheem secured bronze in the men’s S9 100 metres butterfly with a time of 1:03.29, showcasing his upper-body strength, coordination and swimming technique. Their achievements were particularly significant in broadening Sri Lanka’s medal contribution beyond track and field.

Mohamed Safran opened Sri Lanka’s medal account by winning bronze in the men’s T47 long jump with a leap of 6.55 metres. His medal-winning jump came on his final attempt, demonstrating his composure and ability to perform under pressure. Safran’s performance provided an early boost to the team and helped establish momentum for the campaign.

Maduranga Subasinghe also earned bronze in the men’s T47 400 metres, recording a time of 50.03 seconds. His performance reflected his speed endurance and ability to maintain pace over one lap of the track. His medal came after a competitive final in which he was classified alongside Uzbekistan’s Marufojon Morodollove following an evaluation of their equal finishing times. Together, the performances of Safran, Subasinghe and the swimming medallists contributed to Sri Lanka’s final tally of nine medals.

Samitha Dulan, Sri Lanka’s javelin thrower and one of the country’s leading para-athletes, narrowly missed a medal in the men’s F44 javelin throw, finishing fourth with a best effort of 64.10 metres. Dulan, the team captain, who won silver at the 2024 Paris Paralympics with a world-record throw of 67.03 metres in the F44 classification, had been among Sri Lanka’s strongest medal prospects. His fourth-place finish in Nagoya was a disappointment, although it did not diminish his standing as an accomplished international competitor.

Sri Lanka’s overall performance becomes more meaningful when compared with previous editions of the Asian Para Games. At the 2018 Games in Jakarta, Sri Lanka won 14 medals, comprising four gold, six silver and four bronze, finishing 14th in the medal standings. Athletics was the principal contributor, accounting for 13 medals, while wheelchair tennis provided the remaining bronze. The 2018 campaign therefore remains a benchmark for Sri Lanka’s medal-winning potential at the continental level.

At the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, China, Sri Lanka secured 11 medals, including two gold, five silver and four bronze, finishing 18th overall. Pradeep Somasiri won gold in the men’s T46 1,500 metres, while Nuwan Indika Gamage won gold in the men’s T44 100 metres and silver in the long jump. Palitha Bandara also claimed bronze in the shot put. These results demonstrated the importance of experienced athletes and the country’s established strength in para-athletics.

The 2026 campaign showed a mixed but encouraging picture. Sri Lanka’s medal total declined from 11 in 2023 to nine in 2026, yet the country improved its overall position from 18th to 16th. Somasiri successfully defended his 1,500-metre title, while Dhananjana emerged as a double medallist with gold in the long jump and silver in the 200 metres. Bandara progressed from bronze to silver in the shot put, and Indika remained among Asia’s leading sprinters. These results suggest that several established athletes continue to improve or maintain their competitive standards, even as the team seeks greater depth across events.

Sri Lanka’s 16th-place finish at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games is therefore both an achievement and a reminder of the work required to progress further. The two gold medals and the Games-record performances of Somasiri and Dhananjana demonstrated the country’s ability to produce athletes capable of reaching the highest level in Asia. However, returning to the top 15 and challenging the 2018 medal benchmark will require sustained investment in athlete development, coaching, sports science, facilities and international competition exposure. Building on the progress made in athletics and swimming, while expanding opportunities in other para-sports, will be essential to Sri Lanka’s ambitions at the next Asian Para Games.

Chasing 242 for victory Pakistan lost their ninth wicket at 154 and England had the game all but wrapped up. But one man refused to give up. Shadab Khan took upon himself to rally the team to a sensational victory scoring his maiden hundred in any format. With last man Haris Rauf, Shadab produced the highest tenth wicket stand in a successful run chase in ODIs – 89* off 80 balls to beat the previous highest of 64* by West Indies pair Deryck Murray and Andy Roberts against Pakistan in the 1975 World Cup.

Pakistan needed 88 to win when Rauf came to the crease. But he hung in there eventually finishing on 7* off 19 balls which included the winning hit for four. Shadab dictated terms from the other end. His maiden ODI hundred was a scintillating, match-winning effort, as England snatched defeat from the jaws of victory for the second match running.

What followed was simply extraordinary, no adjective could do justice to it. From the 36th to the 42nd over, Shadab hit at least one boundary in every over while ensuring Rauf faced no more than two balls per over. When Shadab was on 97, another drama unfolded. He was given out lbw and everyone thought the game was over. But, to everyone’s surprise, UltraEdge picked up a faint inside edge, overturning the decision. Perhaps it was a message from the cricketing gods that this was destined to be Shadab’s day. While tempers flared around him, Shadab remained calm, brought up his maiden international century, and kept finding the boundary with remarkable ease to see Pakistan home.   

England put into bat first were cruising, riding on Ben Duckett’s century until left-arm spinner Arafat Minhas was introduced into the attack in the 29th over as there were two left-handers. He removed Duckett for 105 (111 balls, 10 fours, 2 sixes) and England lost a flurry of wickets to be reduced to 201-9. However, a 40-run stand between Gus Atkinson and Henry Crocombe, pushed the total to 241.

Shaheen Afridi set the tone upfront by striking twice in two overs to remove Tom Banton and Joe Root cheaply. Jordan Cox became the fourth England batter to get dismissed in single-digits as he steered one straight to wide slip. At 52-4, Duckett and Sam Curran stitched an important 93-run stand, But Afridi came back and broke it by bouncing out Curran for 42 (52 balls, 5 fours). Duckett gave a half-chance when he was on 7 when he top-edged a pull off Razaullah and Haris Rauf misjudged by coming in. The left-hander took advantage of it to record his fifth ODI century.

In perfect batting conditions England were left to rue a missed opportunity of posting a big score. They failed to last all 50 overs as Pakistan bowled them out for a below par score with 20 balls spare. Although England›s last pair frustrated Pakistan, all in all it was an outstanding performance from Pakistan. They were brilliant with the ball and sharp in the field.

The private Pool Villas provide secluded two-suite layouts complete with lap pools and rooftop jacuzzis overlooking the ocean.

Art, design and craftsmanship are central to the Aditya experience, from intricately carved bedheads and antique furnishings to statement decorative pieces throughout the property. Beyond the property, guests have access to a curated collection of experiences including whale watching, boat safaris, customised village cycling tours, cookery demonstrations, and guided visits to Galle Fort and nearby cultural attractions.

Now celebrating over two decades of hospitality, Aditya continues to stand apart through its commitment to privacy, personalised service, and experience-led luxury, remaining one of Sri Lanka’s most distinctive boutique beachfront escapes.

Aditya Resort Managing Director Husain Dawoodbhoy said: “Aditya is a labour of love for us and it feels special to be celebrating its 20th anniversary of this unique, boutique hotel. We are so proud to be the front runners of the boutique hospitality space, which Sri Lanka has come to be known for. And we’re thrilled that we have a huge fan base of Aditya loyalists from across the world, who come regularly to experience our beautiful island’s south coast at Aditya.”
